zh:
卷第十
隋天台智者大師說
弟子法慎記
弟子灌頂再治
釋禪波羅蜜修證第七之六
從背捨已去，有六種法門，並屬不壞法道所攝。利根聲聞具此六法，發真無漏，即成不壞法大力阿羅漢，故《摩訶衍》云：「不壞法阿羅漢能具無諍三昧、願智、頂禪。」
en:
Fascicle Ten
Spoken by the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai, of the Sui dynasty
Recorded by his disciple Fashen
Revised and edited by his disciple Guanding
Explaining Dhyāna-Pāramitā's Cultivation and Realization, Topic 7, Part 6

From the eight forms of detachment onward, there are six dharma-gates, all belonging to and included within the non-destructive path. A śrāvaka of sharp faculties, complete with these six dharmas, gives rise to true undefilement and thereby becomes a great-strength arhat of the non-destructive path — hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: "The arhat of the non-destructive path is able to become complete with the samādhi free of contention, the wisdom of aspiration, and the summit dhyāna."

zh: 今分此六種法門，即為四意，謂觀、練、熏、修。一者、背捨及勝處、一切處，此三門並屬觀禪，故《摩訶衍》云：「背捨是初行，勝處是中行，一切處是後行。」悉為對治破根本味禪中無明貪著及淨法愛也。二、九次第定，即是鍊禪；三、師子奮迅三昧，即是熏禪；四、超越三昧，即是修禪。今釋第一、觀禪，即為二意：一、先釋三番修觀禪方法；二、明觀禪功能。第一、釋三番觀行方法者：一、先釋背捨；二、次釋勝處；三、釋一切處也。
en: These six dharma-gates are now divided into four senses, namely: contemplation, refinement, permeation, and cultivation. First, detachment, together with the stations of mastery and the totalities — these three gates all belong to contemplative dhyāna; hence the Mahāyāna treatise says: "Detachment is the initial practice; the stations of mastery are the middle practice; the totalities are the final practice." All three, together, serve as the antidote breaking through the ignorant craving and attachment found within the root dhyānas' own flavor, as well as attachment to the pure dharma itself. Second, the nine sequential concentrations are precisely the refining dhyāna. Third, the lion's-frolic samādhi is precisely the permeating dhyāna. Fourth, the samādhi of transcendence is precisely the cultivating dhyāna.

Explaining the first, contemplative dhyāna, now has two senses: first, explaining in turn the method of cultivating the three tiers of contemplative dhyāna; second, clarifying contemplative dhyāna's own function. First, explaining the method of these three tiers of contemplative practice: first, explaining detachment; second, next explaining the stations of mastery; third, explaining the totalities.

The observe/refine/permeate/cultivate (觀練熏修) framework organizing this entire fascicle gives the non-destructive path a metallurgical logic that the destructive path never needed: where the nine contemplations, eight recollections, and ten perceptions worked by breaking the body's mark outright, the six dharma-gates here work like successive stages of refining a single piece of metal — first shaping it (the three observational gates), then repeatedly re-tempering it until every stage flows into the next without a seam (the nine sequential concentrations), then working it through completely in both directions (the lion's-frolic samādhi), and finally handling it with total freedom of movement (the samādhi of transcendence). This is also the treatise's own final fascicle as it has survived — a point this page returns to in its closing status note.

items.en: The Eight Forms of Detachment: Naming, Stages, and Method
items.zh: 八背捨 · 釋名 · 次位 · 觀法不同

zh: 先釋八背捨。八背捨者：一、內有色相外觀色，是初背捨；二、內無色相外觀色，是二背捨；三、淨背捨身作證，是三背捨；四、虛空處背捨；五、識處背捨；六、不用處背捨；七、非有想非無想背捨；八、滅受想背捨。今釋背捨，即為五意：一、釋名；二、明次位；三、辯觀法不同；四、明修證；五、分別趣道之相。
en: First, explaining detachment. The eight forms of detachment are: first, form within, contemplating form without — this is the first detachment; second, no form within, contemplating form without — this is the second detachment; third, the pure detachment realized in the body — this is the third detachment; fourth, the detachment of the sphere of space; fifth, the detachment of the sphere of consciousness; sixth, the detachment of the sphere of nothingness; seventh, the detachment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; eighth, the detachment of the cessation of sensation and perception.

Explaining detachment now has five senses: first, explaining the name; second, clarifying the sequence of stages; third, distinguishing the differing contemplative methods across schools; fourth, clarifying cultivation and realization; fifth, distinguishing the mark of how it leads toward the path.

zh: 第一、釋名。此八法門所以通名背捨者，背是淨潔五欲，離是著心，故名背捨。言淨潔五欲者，欲界麁弊色、聲、香、味、觸，貪著是法，沈沒三塗，名為不淨五欲。欲界定、未到地、根本四禪、四空，是中雖生味著，皆名淨潔五欲。今以背捨、無漏對治，破除厭離，不著欲界根本禪定喜樂，故言能背是淨潔五欲，捨是著心，名為背捨。復次，多有人言：「背捨即是解脫之異名。」今用《摩訶衍》意往撿，此義不然。所以者何？如《大品經》云：「菩薩依八背捨，入九次第定。」身證阿那含人雖得九次第定，而不得受具足八解之名。故知因中厭離煩惱，名背捨；後具足觀、鍊、熏、修，發真無漏，三界結盡，爾時背捨轉名解脫。如此說者，義則可依。
en: First, explaining the name: as for why these eight dharma-gates are, in general, named detachment — "turning one's back on" refers to the pure and unblemished five desires, and "relinquishing" refers to the attached mind; hence this is named detachment. As for the pure and unblemished five desires: the desire realm's own coarse and debased forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile sensations — craving and clinging to dharmas of this kind causes one to sink into the three evil destinies, and these are named the impure five desires. The desire-realm concentration, the not-yet-arrived state, the root four dhyānas, and the four formless states — though a subtle savoring attachment may still arise within these — are, all together, named the pure and unblemished five desires. Here, through detachment, one uses the undefiled as an antidote, breaking through and removing this attachment, wearying of it and departing from it, no longer clinging to the joy and happiness of the desire realm or of the root dhyāna-concentrations — hence it is said: able to turn one's back on the pure and unblemished five desires, and relinquish the attached mind — this is named detachment.

Furthermore, many people say: "Detachment is itself merely another name for liberation." Examining this now with reference to the sense of the Mahāyāna treatise, this claim does not hold. Why is this? As the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra says: "The bodhisattva, based upon the eight forms of detachment, enters the nine sequential concentrations." The non-returner who has realized this in the body, though he has obtained the nine sequential concentrations, does not yet receive the name of being complete with the eight liberations. Hence one knows: within the cause, wearying of and detaching from affliction is named detachment; only afterward, once complete with contemplation, refinement, permeation, and cultivation, does true undefilement arise, the fetters of the three realms entirely exhausted — at that time, detachment is renamed liberation. Explained in this way, the sense may be relied upon.

zh: 第二、明次位者，解釋不同。若依曇無德人所明，初二背捨，位在欲界；三淨背捨，位在色界四禪；第四、五、六、七，此四背捨，位在四空；第八滅受想背捨，位過三界。若依薩婆多人所說，初二背捨，位通欲界、初禪、二禪；第三淨背捨，唯在四禪。彼云：「三禪樂多，又離不淨近故，不立背捨。」下五背捨，明位不異於前。復有師言：「三禪無勝處，四禪無背捨。」此則與前有異。今依《摩訶衍》中說，論言：「初背捨，初禪攝；第二背捨，二禪攝。」當知此二背捨位在初、二禪中，為對治破欲界故，皆言以是不淨心觀外色。第三、淨背捨位在三禪中，故論云：「淨背捨者，緣淨故淨，遍身受樂，故名身作證。」三界之法，若除三禪，更無遍身之樂。論文又言：「是四禪中有一背一捨、四勝處。」如比上進退從容，當知位在三禪、四禪，苟而遍屬，即互乖論。今若具以此義破射於前，及融通教意，甚自紜紜。下五背捨配位不異於前，今依後家之釋，以辯位次也。
en: Second, clarifying the sequence of stages: the explanations here differ across schools. Following what the Dharmaguptaka masters clarify, the first two detachments are placed at the desire realm; the third, the pure detachment, is placed at the form realm's fourth dhyāna; the fourth through seventh — these four detachments — are placed at the four formless states; and the eighth, the detachment of the cessation of sensation and perception, is placed beyond the three realms entirely. Following what the Sarvāstivādin masters explain, the first two detachments are placed across the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna; the third, the pure detachment, is placed solely at the fourth dhyāna. They say: "Within the third dhyāna, happiness is too abundant, and, moreover, it lies too close to impurity, hence no detachment is established there." The lower five detachments' own stages are explained no differently from before. There is, further, a master who says: "The third dhyāna has no station of mastery; the fourth dhyāna has no detachment" — this, then, differs from what was given before.

Here, following what is explained in the Mahāyāna treatise, the treatise itself says: "The first detachment is included within the first dhyāna; the second detachment is included within the second dhyāna." One should know, then, that these two detachments are placed within the first and second dhyānas, serving as an antidote breaking through the desire realm — in every case it is said that one uses this impure mind to contemplate external form. The third, the pure detachment, is placed at the third dhyāna; hence the treatise says: "The pure detachment takes purity as its object, and is thereby pure, the whole body receiving happiness — hence it is named realization in the body." Among the dharmas of the three realms, apart from the third dhyāna, there is nowhere else where happiness pervades the whole body. The treatise's own text further says: "Within this fourth dhyāna there is one detachment and four stations of mastery" — weighing this passage back and forth with due care, one should know that its own placement spans the third and fourth dhyānas; to assign it wholesale to one alone would run contrary to the treatise's own text. Were one to fully press this sense against what was given before, and attempt to reconcile every school's own teaching, the matter would grow exceedingly tangled. The lower five detachments' own assigned stages are no different from before; here, the later school's own explanation is followed, in order to distinguish the sequence of stages.

zh: 第三、釋觀法不同者，若曇無德人明此八解脫觀，並以空觀而為體；若薩婆多人明此背捨不淨觀，並是有觀，厭背為體。今此八背捨具有事、理兩觀，在因則名背捨，果滿則名解脫，亦名俱解脫也。若偏依前二家所說，此則事、理互有不具，豈得受於俱解脫之名？此中觀行方法與前二家不同，淺深之異，在下自當可見。
en: Third, explaining the differing contemplative methods across schools: following what the Dharmaguptaka masters clarify, these eight liberations' own contemplation takes emptiness-contemplation entirely as its substance; following what the Sarvāstivādin masters clarify, this detachment's own contemplation of impurity is, in every case, a contemplation of concrete existence, taking weariness and turning-away as its substance. Here, these eight forms of detachment are complete with both the contemplation of concrete phenomena and the contemplation of principle together — within the cause, this is named detachment; once the fruit is complete, this is named liberation, also named liberation-in-both-respects. Should one follow, one-sidedly, either of the two schools given above alone, then phenomena and principle would each, mutually, remain incomplete — how, then, could this receive the name of liberation-in-both-respects? The contemplative method given here differs from that of the two schools above; the distinction in relative depth may be seen for itself below.

The treatise's own insistence that "detachment" and "liberation" are not synonyms — the same eight-stage list earning a different name depending on whether the fetters are merely weakened or entirely exhausted — is a recurring habit of this text: taking a term commonly used loosely and re-anchoring it to a precise doctrinal milestone. The cross-school comparison of where each detachment is placed (Dharmaguptaka vs. Sarvāstivādin vs. unnamed other masters) is candid about real disagreement in the tradition, and the treatise's own resolution — that the eight forms of detachment combine both the concrete-phenomena contemplation one school favors and the principle-contemplation the other favors — sets up the "liberation-in-both-respects" (俱解脫) framing that closes fascicle 9's own destructive-path arhat by contrast: the destructive path yields an arhat complete with two kinds of nirvāṇa; the non-destructive path yields one complete in both phenomena and principle.

quiz.q: To which path do the six gates from detachment onward belong, and what does a sharp śrāvaka complete in them become?
options: the non-destructive path; a great-strength arhat of the non-destructive path
quiz.why: The six gates from detachment onward belong to the non-destructive path; a sharp śrāvaka complete in them becomes a great-strength arhat of that path.

quiz.q: The six gates are divided into contemplation, refinement, permeation, and cultivation. Which pairing is correct?
options: detachment, mastery, totalities: contemplation; nine sequential: refinement; lion's frolic: permeation; transcendence: cultivation
quiz.why: Detachment, mastery, and totalities are contemplative dhyāna; the nine sequential concentrations refining; the lion's frolic permeating; transcendence cultivating.

quiz.q: How does the treatise relate detachment, the stations of mastery, and the totalities?
quiz.why: Detachment is the initial practice, the stations of mastery the middle, the totalities the final; all counteract ignorant craving in the root dhyānas and attachment to pure dharma.

quiz.q: What do the three gates of contemplative dhyāna counteract?
options: ignorant craving in the root flavor-dhyānas and attachment to pure dharma
quiz.why: All three counteract the ignorant craving found in the root dhyānas' flavor and attachment to pure dharma.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what can the arhat of the non-destructive path be complete in?
options: the samādhi free of contention, wisdom of aspiration, summit dhyāna
quiz.why: The arhat of the non-destructive path can be complete in the samādhi free of contention, the wisdom of aspiration, and the summit dhyāna.

quiz.q: What are the first three forms of detachment?
options: form within seeing form without; no form within seeing form without; pure detachment realized in the body
quiz.why: The first three are form within contemplating form without; no form within contemplating form without; and the pure detachment realized in the body.

quiz.q: How is the term "detachment" (背捨) explained?
options: turning the back on the pure five desires, relinquishing the attached mind
quiz.why: One turns one's back on the pure five desires, the subtle savoring in the root dhyānas and formless states, and relinquishes the attached mind.

options: the savoring that arises in desire-realm concentration, the not-yet-arrived state, the root dhyānas, and formless states
quiz.why: The coarse sense-objects of the desire realm are the impure five desires; the savoring in desire-realm concentration through the formless states is the pure five desires.

quiz.q: Some say detachment is simply another name for liberation. How does the text judge?
options: no; in the cause it is detachment; once complete and the fetters exhausted, it is renamed liberation
quiz.why: Wearying of affliction in the causal stage is detachment; once complete in the four refinements, with true undefilement and the fetters exhausted, it is renamed liberation.

quiz.q: Who is cited as obtaining the nine sequential concentrations without the name of complete eight liberations?
options: the non-returner realized in the body
quiz.why: The non-returner realized in the body, though attaining the nine sequential concentrations, does not receive the name of complete eight liberations.

quiz.q: According to the Dharmaguptakas, where are the first two detachments and the pure detachment placed?
options: the first two in the desire realm; the pure one in the fourth dhyāna
quiz.why: The Dharmaguptakas place the first two in the desire realm and the pure detachment in the fourth dhyāna. B is the treatise's placement.

quiz.q: Why do the Sarvāstivādins establish no detachment in the third dhyāna?
options: it belongs to the desire realm
happiness is abundant there and it is close to impurity
quiz.why: They say the third dhyāna has too much happiness and is too close to impurity, so no detachment is set there.

quiz.q: How do the Dharmaguptakas and Sarvāstivādins each view the method of detachment?
options: Dharmaguptakas: emptiness-contemplation; Sarvāstivādins: impurity as existence-contemplation and turning away
quiz.why: The Dharmaguptakas take emptiness-contemplation as the substance; the Sarvāstivādins take the impurity contemplation as existence-contemplation with turning away as substance.

quiz.q: How do this text's eight detachments differ from both schools, and why can they be called liberation-in-both-respects?
options: complete in both phenomenal and principle contemplation; either school alone lacks one
quiz.why: These detachments have both phenomenal and principle contemplation; in the cause they are detachment, at full fruition liberation, also called liberation-in-both-respects. Either school alone would leave one side incomplete.
